newsitem.title: UK: UK government urges water firms to manage demand.
newsitem.headline: UK government urges water firms to manage demand.

text.p: Britain's water companies were urged by Environment Secretary John Gummer on Wednesday to manage demand through pricing and reducing leakage in order to reduce the need for new resources.

In a statement announcing publication of a report on "Water Resources and Supply: Agenda for Action," Gummer said demand could be managed by developing "effective and equitable charging arrangements for water supply, and by companies reducing leakage to economic levels."

Responding to a question in the House of Commons, Gummer also said there was a need for dialogue between companies and customers on the balance between security of supply and costs, a point Ofwat head Ian Byatt said in a statemnt he would be considering at the next periodic review of prices.
Byatt said on Tuesday he would review price limits for water companies in 1999, five years ahead of schedule.

Gummer said "a case for new water resource development will be compelling only if there is insufficient scope for deployment of existing resources to meet properly-managed demand." Companies should also consider bulk transfers, he added.

He said the government felt market mechanisms, including price signals, provided an incentive and would publish a consultation paper on economic instruments in relation to water abstraction in early 1997.

But Brian Duckworth, managing director of Severn Trent Water and a spokesman for the Water Services Association which represents water firms, told the Press Association that six new reservoirs would be needed over 20 years to cover demand.

Gummer said it was the responsibility of companies to draw up plans for development of new resources if projected demand could not be managed to stay within the capacity of existing supplies, taking into account climate changes.
The report was commissioned by Gummer in September 1995 after one of the country's worst droughts the previous summer saw water companies cutting non-essential domestic supplies.
At the same time, companies have been heavily criticised for levels of leakage from their pipes, which the opposition Labour Party has estimated to have reached 826 million gallons daily.

Industry watchdog Ofwat welcomed the Environment Department's report and director general Ian Byatt said companies had already submitted strategies to him for promoting efficient use of water by customers.

"The report endorses my view that the extension of selective metering, along with tariff structures that encourage the efficient use of water, has an essential role to play in managing demand," he said in a statement.
Metering is a contentious issue currently as consumer and political groups warning that the worst-off could be hardest hit by charges for amounts of water used.

Byatt said he believed water supplies would be better conserved if companies had a duty, enforced by the regulator, "to show that their charges properly reflect the costs of supply and provide proper incentives for users to use water more efficiently."

Byatt also repeated his call for the government to introduce legislation on compensation by any companies cutting essential domestic supplies, which the government has said it will do when parliamentary time allows.
